title: the hands nobody sees
hookLine: the shoes handed back, the plates scrubbed, the roti rolled by someone you'll never meet; the word for that
tomorrow: the first symbol of the scripture

cards: You leave your shoes at the gurdwara door, and when you come back they're lined up waiting, sometimes wiped clean. Someone scrubbed the plate you ate langar from. Someone rolled the roti.
In the great kitchen in Amritsar, a banker chops onions beside a teenager washing steel plates. Nobody's keeping score, and nobody asks your name. There's a word for what those hands are doing.

teach.b: The word is seva: selfless service, done for others with no reward in mind. Here's what makes it different from just being nice.

teach.h: NOT BESIDE THE PRACTICE. THE PRACTICE.
teach.b: In Sikh life it's part of the spiritual life, not something beside it. The Gurus return to the idea again and again: service done with a humble heart is a way of drawing near to God. Not a warm-up for the real practice.
The practice. Hands in the dishwater count.

And seva has a condition: it's meant to be done without ego. The hymns warn that service done to be seen, thanked or admired quietly turns into something else. That's why so much of it happens where nobody's watching.
The person who scrubbed your plate doesn't know your name, and that isn't an accident.

teach.h: BODY, MIND, AND WHAT YOU HAVE.
teach.b: Sikh teaching names three kinds: with your body, like cooking or cleaning; with your mind, like teaching or listening; and with what you have, like food or money. So there's no one who can't do it.
And if you've seen Sikh volunteers turn up with hot meals after a flood or a fire, now you know the word they'd use.

how: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara by cooking and serving langar, cleaning, washing dishes and looking after shoes, and outside it through relief work and community service, usually as unpaid volunteers.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: seva is a warm-up before the real spiritual practice
in Sikh life it's part of the practice itself. hands in the dishwater count.
much of the work in the Amritsar kitchen is done by volunteers
much of the cooking and washing up is seva: unpaid, and done by people from every walk of life.
seva counts most when people see you do it
the hymns warn that service done to be admired turns into something else. it's meant to be done without ego.

games.q: you've spent the morning scrubbing plates in a gurdwara kitchen. someone asks for your name so they can thank you publicly. what fits seva?
o: give your name and enjoy the thanks.
smile, say it was nothing, and keep washing.
ask them to post about it.
games.why: seva is meant to be done without ego. the whole kitchen runs on people nobody will ever name.

practice: Breathe, and bring to mind one person who could use a hand. Not a grand gesture: a dish, a message, a door held. Picture yourself doing it without telling anyone.
Stay with that picture for a while: one person, one quiet thing.

wordCard.voice: Seva. Selfless service, done without ego, and part of the spiritual life itself. Eighth word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: service, especially service offered freely.

carryVoice: Your line: one quiet thing for someone. Seva works best when nobody hears about it, not even over dinner. Day eight.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, passim (seva and humble service as a way to God)
